entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Giovannino de’ Grassi (died 1398) was a pivotal figure in late 14th-century Lombard art, whose multifaceted talents as an architect, sculptor, painter, and especially as an illuminator, significantly shaped the International Gothic style in Northern Italy. Operating primarily from Milan under the patronage of the powerful Visconti dynasty, particularly Gian Galeazzo Visconti, de’ Grassi’s workshop became a nexus for artistic innovation, bridging the naturalistic tendencies of Northern European art with Italian aesthetic sensibilities. His contributions were crucial in defining the visual culture of the nascent Duchy of Milan and influencing subsequent generations of artists across the Alps, firmly establishing him as a master of the pre-Renaissance era.

De’ Grassi's most celebrated architectural undertaking was his involvement in the foundational stages of the Milan Cathedral (Duomo di Milano), where he served as chief engineer (ingegnere generale) from 1389 until his death. He contributed significantly to the early design and construction, particularly in the planning of the transepts and the choir, leaving a lasting imprint on one of Europe's largest Gothic cathedrals. Beyond architecture, his workshop produced exquisite illuminated manuscripts, notably the *Offiziolo* (Book of Hours of Gian Galeazzo Visconti), a masterpiece completed by Belbello da Pavia after de’ Grassi's death. This manuscript showcases his unparalleled skill in depicting flora, fauna, and human figures with a delicate naturalism and intricate detail, characteristic of the International Gothic idiom, which spread rapidly through artistic centers.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Giovannino de’ Grassi was a leading figure in the development of the International Gothic style, particularly in Italy, influencing artistic trends through his architectural contributions to Milan Cathedral and his highly naturalistic manuscript illuminations. His work provided a crucial bridge between late medieval art and the nascent Renaissance naturalism.
